question_text: You are designing a Foundry project for a medical device manufacturer developing a regulatory submission assistant agent. The agent assists medical writers in creating FDA submission documents by retrieving clinical study data, cross-referencing device specifications, and generating draft technical summaries. All patient data must comply with HIPAA and must never leave the US East region. The team of 10 writers requires 24/7 availability with a P99 latency of under 2 seconds for document generation. AI-generated content must be tracked for auditability, requiring full lineage from source documents to generated sections. The project's initial budget is $8,000/month. Which Foundry architectural design implements security, compliance, and governance requirements?

options.A: Create a hub-based project architecture with a single Foundry resource in US East. Configure private networking by default and ensure all data connections use private endpoints. Deploy regulatory-specific agent instances with dedicated identity managed service identities. Enable content safety filters and configure audit logging to Azure Monitor.
options.B: Create a dedicated Foundry resource per medical writer with individual resource groups. Connect each resource to the corporate VNet using service endpoints. Enable Customer Managed Keys for encryption at rest and enable Microsoft Defender for Foundry. Configure each agent with separate knowledge bases in Azure AI Search.
options.C: Deploy Foundry into an isolated subscription with Azure Policy enforcing HIPAA compliance tagging. Use Azure Private Link to connect to on-premises clinical databases. Configure the agents with built-in tools only and disable Code Interpreter. Create custom roles for writers with read-only access to generated documents.
options.D: Use the multi-tenant Foundry SaaS offering with region pinning to US East. Create a single project for all writers with role-based access controls. Enable data loss prevention policies to mask patient identifiers. Store all prompts in Git repositories with branch protection rules.

question_text: Your financial services company uses Foundry to implement a multi-agent system for processing loan applications. The 'Analyzer' agent extracts applicant information from PDFs, the 'Validator' agent checks data against credit bureau APIs, and the 'Approver' agent makes final decisions. You need to implement a workflow where if the 'Validator' detects discrepancies or missing documents, it must pause and notify a human loan officer via Teams before proceeding, while preserving the full application context. The system must process 5,000 applications daily with individual application state maintained for up to 7 days. Which orchestration approach within Microsoft Agent Framework should you implement?

options.A: Implement magnetic orchestration, creating a primary orchestrator agent that dynamically routes tasks to specialized agents based on content analysis. Configure a 'Human-in-the-loop' tool that posts messages to a Teams channel when validation issues arise and awaits a response before continuing the workflow.
options.B: Implement group chat orchestration where all three agents participate in a shared conversation thread. Configure the 'Validator' agent with a conditional tool that, when triggered by discrepancies, posts a message to a designated Azure Logic App that sends a Teams notification and waits for human input.
options.C: Implement sequential orchestration using the workflow designer, chaining the agents in order. Place a conditional branching step after the 'Validator' agent that, based on validation results, triggers an Azure Function that creates a human task in Azure Boards and suspends the workflow until the task is resolved.
options.D: Implement concurrent orchestration to run the 'Analyzer' and 'Validator' agents simultaneously for speed, followed by the 'Approver' agent. Use the Agent Framework's built-in 'await_human_input' method within the 'Validator's' tool execution logic, which creates a durable pause point in the workflow state.

question_text: A manufacturing quality control agent uses Azure OpenAI GPT-4 Turbo to analyze images from assembly lines and write defect reports. The agent's responses have become increasingly verbose, causing unnecessary details in reports and higher token costs. You need to adapt the model's behavior to produce concise, actionable reports while maintaining factual accuracy and defect classification precision. The solution must not require retraining the underlying foundation model or maintaining separate model deployments for different report styles. Which combination of techniques should you apply?

options.A: Implement supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using a curated dataset of ideal, concise report examples. Use the Foundry portal's fine-tuning workflow with serverless compute, targeting the GPT-4 base model. After fine-tuning, evaluate the new model's groundedness and coherence metrics before deployment.
options.B: Employ prompt engineering by adding a system instruction reinforcing concise reporting, supplemented by few-shot examples of desired output format. Combine this with a post-processing Logic App that uses a smaller, cheaper model (like GPT-3.5-Turbo) to summarize the initial verbose report.
options.C: Apply reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) by collecting ratings from quality engineers on report usefulness. Use the Foundry evaluation SDK to run batch evaluations comparing verbosity scores, then deploy a reward model to guide the agent's generations toward higher-rated outputs.
options.D: Switch the agent's core model from GPT-4 Turbo to a fine-tuned variant of GPT-3.5-Turbo that was previously optimized for technical summarization. Update the agent definition in Foundry to use the new model endpoint and adjust the temperature parameter to reduce creativity.

question_text: Your team manages a Foundry agent that provides customer support via a public web chat. During a red team exercise, an attacker submits a crafted prompt that causes the agent to generate and execute malicious Python code via the Code Interpreter tool, attempting to exfiltrate system environment variables. The attack was successful. You must implement a security control to prevent tool misuse while preserving the agent's legitimate ability to run benign code for calculations and data formatting. What is the MOST effective immediate remediation?

options.A: Disable the Code Interpreter tool for all agents in the Foundry project. Create a custom, secured Azure Function that performs the necessary safe calculations, and expose it to the agent as an OpenAPI tool with strict input validation and output sanitization.
options.B: Enable Content Safety filters at the 'High' threshold for all categories within the Foundry project's safety configurations. Configure the agent's system message to include a directive prohibiting code execution from user requests and audit all tool calls in Azure Monitor.
options.C: Implement a custom pre-evaluation step in the agent's workflow using the Foundry SDK's `add_pre_hook` method. This hook should analyze the user's prompt for risky keywords (like 'import os', 'subprocess') and reject the request before it reaches the model.
options.D: Configure the Code Interpreter tool's sandbox configuration to run in a fully isolated, ephemeral container with no network access and a stripped-down Python environment. Add tool-specific guardrails in the Foundry portal to restrict access to modules like 'os', 'sys', and 'subprocess'.

question_text: A logistics company uses a Foundry agent to optimize delivery routes by analyzing real-time traffic, weather, and package data. The agent's performance has degraded; it now takes 12+ seconds to suggest routes, missing the 5-second SLA. Analysis shows the bottleneck is the RAG retrieval step from an Azure AI Search knowledge base containing 500,000 historical route documents. The agent's grounding score remains high, but latency is unacceptable. Which solution will likely improve retrieval latency while maintaining or improving answer relevance?

options.A: Switch from semantic search to keyword-based hybrid search to reduce embedding computation overhead. Increase the number of search replicas in the Azure AI Search service SKU from 1 to 3 to distribute query load and improve throughput.
options.B: Implement a multi-stage retrieval strategy: first, use a fast, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search with a reduced-dimension embedding model to get a broad candidate set, then re-rank the top candidates using a slower, more accurate cross-encoder model.
options.C: Reduce the chunk size of documents in the knowledge base from 1,000 tokens to 256 tokens to increase the number of searchable chunks. Lower the similarity score threshold in the agent's retrieval tool from 0.7 to 0.5 to ensure enough context is returned for each query.
options.D: Move the knowledge base to a vector database service like Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore with native vector search capabilities, which offers lower latency for similarity searches at scale compared to Azure AI Search's integrated vector support.

question_text: You are tasked with automating the deployment and lifecycle management of Foundry agents across development, staging, and production environments for a team of 15 AI engineers. The process must include: 1) automated provisioning of Foundry resources using Infrastructure-as-Code, 2) CI/CD for agent definitions and prompts stored in GitHub, 3) automated quality and safety evaluations triggered on each pull request, and 4) progressive rollout (canary deployment) of new agent versions to a percentage of production traffic. Which combination of Azure services and Foundry features accomplishes this?

options.A: Use Azure DevOps pipelines with Bicep templates for Foundry resource deployment. Store agent YAML definitions and prompts in a Git repository. Use GitHub Actions workflows that call the Foundry Evaluation SDK to run batch evaluations on test datasets. Implement progressive rollout by deploying the agent to a separate Foundry project endpoint and using Azure Traffic Manager to split traffic.
options.B: Use Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates and the Azure CLI to deploy Foundry projects into each environment. Integrate the Foundry Git connector to sync prompts and flows from a GitHub repository branch. Configure Azure Monitor alerts for safety metric thresholds. Perform canary releases by manually updating a percentage of user sessions in the application front-end to use a new agent version tag.
options.C: Use Foundry Projects' built-in environment promotion feature to move validated agents from Dev to Prod. Store all prompts in the Foundry Portal's prompt management system with version history. Configure automated evaluations in the portal using a pre-defined test dataset and quality metrics. Use the agent deployment settings to specify a percentage rollout for the new agent version.
options.D: Use Terraform to define Foundry resources and Azure Pipelines for CI/CD. Store agent configurations as JSON files in Azure Repos. Use Azure Machine Learning's evaluation capabilities to assess agent performance. Implement canary testing by creating two agent instances in production and using an Azure Function as a router to direct a percentage of requests to the new version.

question_text: An e-commerce company uses a Foundry agent with a large product catalog knowledge base in Azure AI Search to answer customer questions. The agent's answers are often not grounded in the catalog, hallucinating product features or prices. You have enabled the groundedness metric in evaluations, which confirms a 30% hallucination rate. The knowledge base uses the default text-embedding-ada-002 model. Team analysis suggests the retrieval step is failing to find the most relevant product documents due to domain-specific terminology. What is the most targeted action to improve groundedness?

options.A: Fine-tune the text-embedding-ada-002 model on a dataset of product descriptions and customer queries from your domain. Use the Foundry fine-tuning service with managed compute, then update the knowledge base index to use the new custom embedding model for both indexing and querying.
options.B: Increase the 'Top N' documents retrieved by the agent's search tool from 5 to 20 to provide more context to the LLM, even if some documents are less relevant. Also, add a system prompt instruction reminding the model to only answer based on the provided search results.
options.C: Switch to a different, larger general-purpose embedding model available in the Foundry catalog, such as text-embedding-3-large, and re-index the entire knowledge base. Implement hybrid search (keyword + semantic) to combine the strengths of BM25 and vector search.
options.D: Implement a re-ranking step after the initial retrieval. Use a cross-encoder model (like a small BERT model fine-tuned on relevance) to re-score the top 50 retrieved documents and select the top 5 most relevant ones to pass to the LLM for answer generation.

question_text: You are configuring cost management for a portfolio of 50 Foundry agents used internally by a large enterprise. Agents have varying usage patterns; some are used constantly by thousands of employees, while others are triggered only by specific events a few times per day. Finance requires detailed, agent-level token consumption breakdowns and monthly cost forecasts to stay within a $50,000 monthly budget. They also want alerts if any single agent's projected monthly cost exceeds $5,000. How should you implement cost monitoring and alerting?

options.A: Use Azure Cost Management's cost analysis for the Foundry resource group. Create budgets with resource group scope and configure alerts based on actual cost. Use tags on each Foundry project to identify different departments, but agent-level breakdown requires custom logging.
options.B: Enable Diagnostic Settings for the Foundry resource to emit logs to a Log Analytics workspace. Create a KQL query to parse the logs, sum token usage per agent ID, and calculate costs. Build an Azure Dashboard with cost per agent and use an Alert Rule based on the KQL query result to trigger notifications.
options.C: Use the Foundry portal's built-in cost analytics dashboard, which provides per-agent, per-model token consumption and estimated cost. Configure budget alerts within the portal's Project Settings for each agent, sending email notifications to the finance team when thresholds are breached.
options.D: Implement a custom telemetry solution using the Foundry SDK to instrument each agent call, recording token counts to Application Insights. Create Power BI reports from Application Insights data to visualize costs. Set up Azure Monitor alerts based on custom metrics ingested from Application Insights.

question_text: A software company's Foundry agent assists developers by generating code snippets from natural language descriptions in their IDE. The agent uses the Code Interpreter tool to execute the generated Python code in a sandbox and verify its correctness. Security audit findings reveal that the sandbox environment persists between user sessions, potentially allowing a malicious user to write a file in one session and read it in another, violating isolation requirements. How should you reconfigure the tool to enforce session isolation?

options.A: In the Foundry project's Tool Configuration, locate the Code Interpreter tool settings and enable the 'Ephemeral Sessions' option. This ensures a fresh, clean sandbox environment is created for each new user conversation thread, with no persistence of files or state between threads.
options.B: Disable the built-in Code Interpreter tool. Develop a custom Azure Function that acts as a secure code executor. The function should spin up a new, isolated Docker container for each request, execute the code, return the output, and then destroy the container, guaranteeing isolation.
options.C: Modify the agent's system prompt to include a directive that clears the working directory at the start of each user interaction. Rely on the LLM to generate and execute a command like 'rm -rf *' before running the user's requested code, thereby resetting the environment.
options.D: Continue using the built-in tool but configure an Azure Logic App that runs on a schedule (e.g., every 10 minutes) to call a management API that resets all active sandbox environments across the Foundry project, purging any persistent files or state.

question_text: Your team is scaling a Foundry-based customer service agent from handling 100 to 10,000 concurrent conversations. The agent uses GPT-4 with a 128K context window and integrates with a CRM via an OpenAPI tool. Performance tests show the P99 latency increasing from 1.5s to 8s under load, primarily due to model API call latency. You need to maintain the SLA of under 3 seconds while controlling costs. Budget allows for a 2x increase in monthly inference spend. Which scaling configuration should you implement?

options.A: Switch from the serverless API to deploying the GPT-4 model on a Provisioned Throughput Unit (PTU) with capacity reserved for your Foundry project. Configure the PTU tier based on your peak concurrent request forecast to guarantee lower latency and higher throughput.
options.B: Implement a model cascade strategy: configure the agent to first call a faster, cheaper model (like GPT-3.5-Turbo). Only if the confidence score of the initial response is below a threshold (based on a custom evaluator), route the request to the more capable but slower GPT-4 model for a second attempt.
options.C: Increase the number of parallel asynchronous agent runs by scaling the Foundry Agent Service's compute configuration. Use the SDK to implement request batching, where multiple user queries are aggregated into a single, larger API call to the LLM to improve efficiency and reduce per-request overhead.
options.D: Enable response caching in the Foundry Agent configuration. Configure a Redis cache to store agent responses indexed by a hash of the user query and conversation context. Serve cached responses for identical queries, bypassing the LLM call entirely for repeat questions.
